subject: english-literature
topicDisplay: Unit 2 The Study Of Poetry 1900 Present And Drama 1900 Present
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Modernist poetry of the early twentieth century is frequently marked by:
options: Regular metre, full rhyme and reassuring closure
Pastoral celebration of an unspoilt countryside
Fragmentation, allusion, free verse and a sense of disorientation
questions.explain: Modernist work such as Eliot's often uses fragmentation, dense allusion and free verse to register a fractured modern world.

questions.q: The phrase 'literature does not exist in a vacuum' captures the principle that:
options: Texts should be read without any reference to the world
Texts are produced and read within social, historical and ideological conditions that bear on their meaning
Only science is shaped by context
questions.explain: This principle underpins AO3: texts are embedded in, and engage with, their world.

questions.q: The repetition of vowel sounds within nearby words, as in 'fleet feet sweep', is termed:
questions.explain: Assonance is the patterning of internal vowel sounds, creating cohesion or musicality.

questions.q: Wilfred Owen's stated aim that 'the Poetry is in the pity' signals that his war poetry seeks to:
options: Convey compassion for the suffering of soldiers and protest war's waste
questions.explain: Owen foregrounds pity and protest, exposing the human cost of war rather than glorifying it.

questions.q: Modernism as a literary context responds to 'modern times' by registering:
options: A sense of fragmentation, alienation and the breakdown of old certainties after industrialisation and war
Confidence in steady moral and social progress
questions.explain: Modernist writing reflects a fractured, disorientating modernity, often through fragmented form and alienated voices.

questions.q: A defining preoccupation of Romantic poetry (Wordsworth, Coleridge, Keats) is:
options: Strict adherence to the three dramatic unities
The imagination, nature and intense subjective feeling
questions.explain: Romanticism foregrounds imagination, nature, emotion and the individual sensibility against Enlightenment rationalism.

questions.q: An ode is traditionally a poem that is:
options: A serious, elevated lyric addressed to a person, thing or abstraction
A 14-line love poem with a couplet
A brief, witty epigram of two lines
A narrative folk song with a refrain
questions.explain: The ode is a dignified, often celebratory lyric of address, as in Keats's odes to a nightingale or a Grecian urn.

questions.q: The idea that context shapes a text's 'reception' means that:
options: Reception is irrelevant to literary study
How readers interpret and value a text changes with their own historical and cultural situation
Texts mean exactly the same to every reader in every era
Context only affects the author, never readers
questions.explain: Reception theory recognises that meaning and value are shaped by the reader's own context, not fixed forever.

questions.q: A villanelle is a fixed form notable for which feature?
options: Fourteen lines split into octave and sestet
An unrhymed line of five iambic feet
Two refrains repeated across nineteen lines in five tercets and a quatrain
A single eight-line stanza with a couplet turn
questions.explain: The villanelle has nineteen lines, five tercets and a closing quatrain, woven around two recurring refrains.

questions.q: An extended, often surprising metaphor that yokes together strikingly unlike ideas, characteristic of Donne and the Metaphysicals, is a:
questions.explain: The metaphysical conceit develops an elaborate, intellectually ingenious comparison across the poem.

questions.q: Studying literature 'in shared contexts' assumes that grouping texts by context helps reveal:
options: That all texts of a period are identical
Patterns, dialogues and contrasts in how writers respond to the same conditions
questions.explain: Clustering by context illuminates how different writers engage, variously, with shared circumstances.

questions.q: The contextual study of gender in literature considers how texts may:
options: Either reinforce or subvert the gender expectations of their period
questions.explain: Texts can both uphold and challenge the gender norms of their time, and analysis should weigh which.

questions.q: In 'texts in shared contexts', comparing a text written during an event with one written long after it allows students to explore:
options: How temporal distance and hindsight shape representation of the same context
questions.explain: Contemporary and retrospective treatments of the same context reveal how perspective and hindsight alter representation.

questions.q: Rhyme that occurs within a single line rather than at line-endings is called:
questions.explain: Internal rhyme places rhyming words within the same line, adding density and momentum.

questions.q: A line of iambic pentameter contains how many metrical feet, and of what basic pattern?
options: Six feet, each a stressed-then-unstressed trochee
Five feet, each an unstressed-then-stressed iamb
questions.explain: Iambic pentameter is five iambs per line, each iamb being an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one.

questions.q: The 'changing role of women' as a shared context allows study of how literature reflects and shapes shifts in:
options: Women's social, legal and economic status across periods
questions.explain: Texts can be read against evolving expectations, rights and roles of women over time.

questions.q: To say a text is shaped by its 'context of production' is to consider:
options: The historical, social and personal circumstances in which it was written
The price of the first edition
Only how modern readers respond to it
questions.explain: Context of production concerns the conditions under which a work was created, distinct from its later reception.

questions.q: Which group of poets is most associated with wit, paradox and elaborate conceits in the early seventeenth century?
questions.explain: Donne, Herbert and Marvell are central Metaphysical poets, known for intellectual conceits and dramatic argument.

questions.q: A pair of words such as 'love' and 'remove' (a fuller rhyme in Shakespeare's day, now imperfect) illustrates what poets and critics call a:
questions.explain: Half-rhyme (or slant/para-rhyme) approximates rather than fully matches the sound, a device prominent in Owen and Dickinson.

questions.q: When comparing two poems' methods and ideas, the most analytically rewarding approach is to:
options: Compare how each poet uses form and language to treat a shared concern, weighing similarity and difference
Describe one poem fully, then the other, with no link
Decide which poet was more famous
questions.explain: Effective comparison is integrated, examining how each text's methods shape its treatment of a common theme.

questions.q: A Petrarchan sonnet characteristically divides into an octave and a sestet, and the turn between them is known as the:
questions.explain: The volta is the 'turn' in thought or argument, conventionally falling between the octave and sestet of a Petrarchan sonnet.

questions.q: The repetition of consonant sounds, especially at the ends or middles of words, as in 'pitter-patter', is:
questions.explain: Consonance is the repetition of consonant sounds; assonance, by contrast, repeats vowel sounds.

questions.q: In the context of 'modern times', T. S. Eliot's 'The Waste Land' is frequently read as expressing:
options: The spiritual barrenness and fragmentation of post-war modern civilisation
questions.explain: Eliot's fragmented, allusive poem is read as diagnosing the sterility and disorder of the modern world.

questions.q: Recognising that an interpretation is itself shaped by the critic's context means accepting that:
options: Critical readings (e.g. Marxist, feminist, post-colonial) reflect particular values and questions
There is only one timeless 'correct' reading
questions.explain: Critical approaches are themselves historically and ideologically situated, generating different readings.

questions.q: 'Protest' or political writing is characterised by its intention to:
options: Challenge injustice, power or oppression and provoke the reader to question the status quo
Describe nature for its own sake
questions.explain: Protest literature is purposive, contesting injustice and inviting critique of prevailing power.

questions.q: A poem spoken throughout by a single character who is not the poet, addressing a silent listener, is a:
questions.explain: The dramatic monologue, perfected by Browning, has one speaker distinct from the poet revealing themselves to a silent auditor.

questions.q: In scansion, a foot of two consecutive stressed syllables is called a:
questions.explain: A spondee consists of two stressed syllables, often used to slow or weight a line.

questions.q: The literature of the First World War (Owen, Sassoon) is often distinguished from earlier patriotic verse by its:
options: Unflinching depiction of suffering, futility and disillusionment
Avoidance of any reference to combat
Celebration of war's glory and heroism
questions.explain: Owen and Sassoon expose the horror and futility of trench warfare, countering older glorifying conventions.

questions.q: AO3 (context) is best handled in an essay by:
options: Adding a separate paragraph of historical facts unconnected to the text
Listing every event of the period
Weaving relevant context into analysis to illuminate how it shapes the text's meaning and reception
questions.explain: Strong AO3 use integrates context with close analysis rather than treating it as a detachable 'bolt-on'.

questions.q: When applying context, the strongest essays treat historical material as:
options: A lens that illuminates specific choices of language, form and meaning in the text
A fixed set of facts to be recited at the start
A substitute for reading the text
questions.explain: Context works best as an interpretive lens tied to particular textual details, not recitation.
